stages.title: Short stories
stages.hook: A whole story in a few pages: what must a writer leave out, and what must stay?
explain: A short story is a brief work of fiction, usually read in one sitting. It focuses on one main event or idea, has few characters, and moves quickly to a point. Because space is tight, every detail should matter.

The American writer Edgar Allan Poe argued that a short story should aim at a single effect. The Russian writer Anton Chekhov showed how a small moment can reveal a whole life, and Rabindranath Tagore wrote short stories in Bengali about ordinary people in India.

Many short stories end with a twist or with irony, when the outcome is the opposite of what is expected. In O. Henry's The Gift of the Magi, a poor couple each sell a treasure to buy a gift for the other, and each gift becomes useless, yet the story shows their love.

example.q: Why does the twist in The Gift of the Magi work?
steps: Each partner sacrifices a prized thing.
Each gift fits the thing the other sold.
The reader sees the irony: the gifts cannot be used, yet the love is clear.
example.a: Irony: the result is the opposite of what was planned, but it reveals love.

analogies.home: A short story is like a single family photograph rather than a whole album.
analogies.city: A story can fit in a train journey.
analogies.music: A short story is like a single song, not an album.
analogies.tech: It is like a short film, not a series.

stages.mnemonic: Short story: one moment, few people, one punch.
terms: A brief fiction focused on one event or idea.

misc.wrong: A short story is just a shortened novel.
misc.right: It is a form of its own, with a tight focus and few characters, not a summary of something longer.

stages.limits: Definitions of short story vs novella vary, mostly by length.

stages.title: Novels and narrative structure
stages.hook: Why does a novel give us time to know a character in a way a short story cannot?
explain: A novel is a long work of fiction. Its length lets writers build detailed characters, several plot lines (subplots) and whole worlds. Early landmark novels include The Tale of Genji, written in Japan by Murasaki Shikibu around the early 11th century, and Don Quixote, by Miguel de Cervantes, published in 1605 and 1615.

Narrative structure is how the story is organised: chapters, the order of events, flashbacks and the point of view. First person uses I. Third person limited follows one character's thoughts. An omniscient narrator knows everything about everyone.

Narrative voice shapes meaning. An unreliable narrator may be biased or mistaken, so readers must read between the lines. Structures vary: some novels tell events in order, others use a frame story or jump between times.

example.q: Identify the point of view: "I ran to the gate, my heart pounding."
steps: The narrator is a character in the story.

analogies.home: Hearing a story from a family member vs hearing it from a neighbour changes what you learn.
analogies.city: Two witnesses of an accident give different accounts.
analogies.sport: A commentator who knows every player is like an omniscient narrator.
analogies.tech: A video blog is first person; a documentary is third person.

terms: A long work of fiction, usually in prose.
The perspective from which a story is told.
A smaller story line alongside the main plot.

misc.right: The narrator is a voice created by the author, who may be a character with their own limits.

stages.limits: Which book is the first novel is debated and depends on how novel is defined.

stages.title: Poetry forms and imagery
stages.hook: Fourteen lines, three lines, five lines: how does the shape of a poem change what it can say?
explain: Poems come in forms. A sonnet has 14 lines. A haiku is a very short Japanese form that traditionally has 17 sounds in three lines of 5, 7 and 5 and often points to a season. A limerick is a funny five-line poem rhyming AABBA. A ballad tells a story in verse. Free verse has no regular rhyme or metre.
Imagery is language that appeals to the senses: sight, sound, smell, taste and touch. "The bread smelt warm and sweet" gives smell and touch. Strong imagery makes the reader feel they are there.
Poems can also use figurative language, tone and sound. The Japanese poet Matsuo Bashō (1644-1694) wrote famous haiku about nature, such as the old pond and the frog.

example.q: Count the syllables of a haiku line: "An old silent pond" (5 sounds?).
steps: The first line of a haiku is 5.

analogies.home: A lullaby is a simple poem sung at home.
analogies.city: Street signs use short punchy words, like very short poems.
analogies.nature: A haiku captures a single moment in nature.
analogies.music: A ballad is a song-like poem that tells a story.

stages.title: Drama and dialogue
stages.hook: In a play, how does an audience learn what a character is thinking without a narrator?
explain: Drama relies on dialogue, the speech between characters. Good dialogue reveals character, moves the plot and shows relationships. What is not said can matter too; that hidden meaning is called subtext.

Plays have special speech types. A monologue is a long speech by one character. A soliloquy is spoken when a character is alone, so the audience hears their inner thoughts. An aside is a short remark to the audience that other characters do not hear.

Scripts also include stage directions, written in italics or brackets, which describe movement, tone and setting. A play is split into acts and scenes. Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something that a character does not.

example.q: What is the effect of an aside: (to audience) "I am not as honest as I seem."
steps: We learn the truth they hide.

analogies.home: Whispering a secret in front of others who cannot hear is like an aside.
analogies.city: Overhearing one side of a phone call shows how dialogue reveals more than we are told.
analogies.sport: A coach's pep talk is a monologue.
analogies.music: An aria in opera is like a soliloquy in song.

misc.right: Tone, pauses and what is left unsaid (subtext) carry meaning too.

stages.title: Ancient Greek drama
stages.hook: Why would a whole city stop work to watch plays? That is what happened in ancient Athens.
explain: Theatre in the West grew in ancient Greece. In Athens, plays were performed at festivals for Dionysus, the god of wine and theatre, in large open-air theatres cut into hillsides. Actors wore masks, and a chorus of singers and dancers commented on the action.

Three great tragedians survive: Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides. Sophocles' Oedipus the King is about a ruler who searches for the cause of a plague in his city and uncovers a painful truth about himself. Sophocles' Antigone is about a young woman who chooses to follow her family duty against the ruler's order. Tragedy usually shows a noble person brought low by a flaw or by fate.

Comedy was written too. Aristophanes wrote comedies full of jokes and satire about Athenian life, such as The Clouds and The Frogs. The philosopher Aristotle, in his Poetics, described tragedy as arousing pity and fear and leading to catharsis, an emotional release.

example.q: Why did the Greek theatre have a chorus?
steps: They sang and danced between scenes.
They commented on events and spoke for the community.
example.a: The chorus guided the audience's reaction.

analogies.home: A family chorus cheering at a game is like a chorus.
analogies.city: City-wide festivals bring people together as Athens did.
analogies.sport: A stadium crowd's chant echoes the chorus.

stages.title: Introduction to Shakespeare
stages.hook: He left no diary and wrote no letters we have. How do we know so much about the world's most performed playwright?
explain: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, in 1564 and died in 1616. He wrote about 37 plays and 154 sonnets, and acted with a company at the Globe Theatre in London. After his death, friends published the First Folio in 1623, which saved many plays that might have been lost.

His plays are grouped as tragedies (such as Hamlet and Macbeth), comedies (such as A Midsummer Night's Dream) and histories (such as Henry V). Late in his career he wrote romances such as The Tempest.

Much of his writing is in blank verse, unrhymed lines with a pattern of ten syllables, called iambic pentameter, a rhythm like da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM. His language added many phrases to English. Famous lines include "To be, or not to be, that is the question" from Hamlet and "All the world's a stage" from As You Like It.

example.q: Count the syllables in "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" (Shakespeare, Sonnet 18).
steps: Split it: Shall I / com-PARE / thee TO / a SUM / mer's DAY.
example.a: Ten syllables in five beats: iambic pentameter.

analogies.home: Plays were performed for ordinary Londoners, not just rich people.

analogies.music: Iambic rhythm is like a heartbeat: da-DUM.

stages.title: Myths and legends of Africa and Europe
stages.hook: Why do dragons, heroes and tricksters appear in so many ancient stories?
explain: Myths explain how the world began, why seasons change or how heroes act. Legends are stories about heroes or events that may be rooted in real history but grow with retelling. Both were passed on by mouth for a long time before they were written down.

In Africa, the Epic of Sundiata tells of a prince who overcame difficulties to found the Mali Empire. Amazigh peoples of North Africa tell tales of clever villagers and wise elders. In Europe, Norse mythology speaks of the god Odin, the hammer-wielding Thor and the world tree Yggdrasil. The Arthurian legends tell of King Arthur, the Round Table and the knights who served him. Slavic folklore has Baba Yaga, a witch who lives in a hut on chicken legs.

Myths and legends show what communities value, such as loyalty, courage and cleverness. Different peoples sometimes tell similar tales, which may come from shared human concerns or from travelling stories.

example.q: Decide if it is myth or legend: Thor swings his hammer to guard the gods.
steps: The tale explains the power of thunder in Norse belief.

analogies.home: Grandparents retell legends of local heroes.

stages.title: Asian and American literary traditions
stages.hook: An epic can be longer than a novel and still be sung or recited. Which Asian and American epics shaped whole cultures?
explain: India has two great Sanskrit epics. The Ramayana, traditionally credited to the sage Valmiki, tells of Prince Rama, his wife Sita and the loyal Hanuman. The Mahabharata, traditionally credited to Vyasa, is among the longest poems in the world and includes the Bhagavad Gita. In Persia, Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh, the Book of Kings, around the year 1010.

In China, Journey to the West follows the monk Xuanzang and the Monkey King Sun Wukong. In Japan, Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, and Bashō perfected haiku. The Arabic One Thousand and One Nights is a frame story told by Scheherazade.

In the Americas, the K'iche' Maya recorded the Popol Vuh. The Inca told stories of their origins, and the Guaraní and Mapuche of South America tell tales of nature and spirits. In North America, Inuit and many Native nations have rich oral literatures, African American communities developed rich folktales, and Mark Twain's novels shaped American literature.

example.q: Name the epic: "Rama, Sita and Hanuman".

analogies.home: Families in India share the Ramayana through plays and tales at festivals.
analogies.city: Temples and cities host Ramayana performances in several Asian countries.

stages.title: Australian and Pacific storytelling traditions
stages.hook: How did islanders cross thousands of kilometres of ocean without a map? Their stories were part of the answer.
explain: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia have the world's oldest continuing storytelling traditions. Stories, songs, dance and art together carry knowledge of country, law and living things. Some stories are open to everyone and others are restricted, so we only learn those shared publicly.

In Polynesia, navigators crossed the Pacific using stars, ocean swells, winds and birds, and passed this knowledge on through chants and stories. The Māori tell of Rangi, the sky father, and Papa, the earth mother, who were pushed apart by their son Tāne so that light could enter the world. Hawaiians share legends of Māui and of ancestors who sailed to the islands.

Pacific storytelling often links people to ancestors and to place. A story may explain a mountain, a reef or a family's connection to land. This is why good storytellers name the community a story belongs to and use it with care.

steps: Chants stored star paths, swells and bird signs.
Telling and chanting helped them remember.

analogies.home: Family stories link people to their ancestors and places.
analogies.sea: Wayfinders memorised star paths in chants.
